law_discussed: ICT Act 2006; DSA 2018; Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Sub-inspectors face internal barriers (little tech/logistics at station level, shallow cyber training, non-investigative duty load) and external ones (victim non-cooperation from shame, bKash and Facebook slow or refusing to share data, SIMs registered on others' NIDs, volatile digital evidence, cross-jurisdiction offenders).
prevalence_reported: Cites Dhaka Cyber Tribunal 2013-2020: 2,669 cases, 768 disposed, 22 convictions (2.86%); ~80% of victims unsatisfied with police (CCAF 2023) - secondary figures
author_gaps: Perspective of specialised units and victims not covered; small convenience sample
recommendations: Station-level cyber tools; cyber/digital-forensics modules in Sardah training; regular in-service training; staffing; police-private sector (MFS, platform) cooperation; curb fraudulent SIM registration
quality_note: Small sample (n=8), all male SIs, two districts; clear methods; author is criminologist (PhD on cyber violence victimisation) - possible supervisor/collaborator contact

key_findings: Curated ~50k Bangla/English/Banglish SMS (fraud vs legitimate, from Facebook scam reports and volunteers); Bangla-BERT-base best (91% accuracy, recall 100%, precision 85.5%); prototype app shows pop-up scam warnings.
author_gaps: No public Bangla fraud-SMS dataset existed; no formal user testing of alerts
quality_note: Internal inconsistencies (conclusion describes emotion detection; recall 100% for all models implausible); technical only

population: university students; police or justice actors
theory: none (trust in automation / appropriate reliance framing)
key_findings: 77% cautious about treating digital media as authentic, 64% say legal professionals need stronger deepfake-evaluation skills, 56% aware AI can fabricate media; awareness weakly/not associated with endorsing training. Argues provenance, authentication and evidentiary weight should be trained separately (Evidence Act ss 65A-65B).
author_gaps: No measure of actual detection skill; non-probability sample dominated by law students; test practitioners with case tasks; pre-post training evaluation
recommendations: Case-based legal training on provenance, preservation and interpreting forensic reports
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset used in companion papers (R0022 likely) - not independent; GenAI-assisted drafting disclosed; careful statistics

key_findings: 49% recognised AI misuse for phishing/impersonation, 81% verify unusual requests, 82% use security practices; awareness not associated with protective behaviour after adjustment, daily AI use was.
author_gaps: Need validated measures and behavioural (not self-report) outcomes; prospective designs
recommendations: Distinguish recognition, detection confidence and behaviour in university cyber education
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset as R0015 - not independent sample

key_findings: XGBoost best on synthetic PaySim mobile-money data (F1 0.54, PR-AUC 0.57); calibration and SHAP explanations; top-1% adaptive alerting cuts false positives 39% but halves recall.
author_gaps: No real Bangladeshi MFS/bank transaction data available; validation on governed local data needed
recommendations: Bangladesh Bank e-KYC guidance should encourage chronological validation and explainable, capacity-aware alerting
quality_note: Uses NO Bangladesh data - evidence of data-access gap for MFS fraud research

key_findings: CSA 2026's vague offences ('defamatory online content', 'false information', 'cyber propaganda', 'cyber terrorism') fail ICCPR Art 19(3) legality/necessity/proportionality; ss 31-36 allow device/traffic access without judicial warrant; chilling effect; compared with US First Amendment, EU DSA and Shreya Singhal (India). Fails all five tests for sound cyber legislation.
recommendations: Five reform principles: narrow definitions, judicial warrants, proportionate penalties, independent oversight, decriminalise defamation
quality_note: Undergraduate-authored; low-tier journal (IRE); some garbled text

key_findings: Bangladesh lacks treaty networks (not party to Budapest Convention), relies on slow MLATs, has outdated digital-evidence and data-access procedures; compared with US CLOUD Act and EU EIO/e-Evidence, causing investigative delays in transnational cases (e.g. 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist).
recommendations: Harmonised cybercrime definitions; streamlined MLATs; digital evidence reform; capacity building; accede to Budapest Convention

location: national (comparative: EU, Italy, UK, US, China, S Korea, India, Bangladesh)
law_discussed: CSA 2026 / Ordinance 2025 (as coded in index); Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Leximetric Synthetic Media Legal Coverage Index: Bangladesh scored lowest (6/18, 33%) vs US 15/18; sexual-deepfake offences widely covered, likeness/licensing rights least. Proposes four-layer model (right, licence, transparency, liability) for Bangladesh.
recommendations: Dignity-based personality right with copyright as enforcement container; transparency and platform duties
quality_note: Author based in India; journal (Int J Special Education) off-topic outlet; Bangladesh is one of 8 cases but scored and targeted by recommendations

key_findings: 2017 India-Bangladesh CERT MoU (CERT-In / BGD e-GOV CIRT) is weak because Art 5 defers to divergent national laws; no binding standards, oversight or law-enforcement integration. Proposes AI tools for harmonisation and joint threat intelligence.
prevalence_reported: Cites secondary figures: DMP 2023 23.9% of cyber cases Facebook breaches/extortion/fraud; '73% of Bangladeshi women experienced cybercrime' (unsourced)
recommendations: Operationalise MoU Art 5 with joint protocols, cyber exercises, shared AI-based threat classification and evidence standards
quality_note: Indian political science author; low-tier journal; largely descriptive, weakly sourced statistics

key_findings: DSA 2018 (and Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act 2015) use vague offences ('false', 'offensive', 'defamatory') enabling selective enforcement against journalists/activists; misinformation used to justify censorship; opaque state-platform takedowns; Bangladesh enforcement more centralised and systematic than Nigeria's.
author_gaps: Desk-based; no interviews or enforcement data
recommendations: Narrow definitions; independent multi-stakeholder digital regulator; platform transparency; media literacy over punishment; rights-based data protection
quality_note: Nigerian ICT agency authors; several references look unverifiable (possible fabricated citations); secondary sources only

key_findings: 55% see AI misuse as 'very common', women and children seen as most vulnerable; 65% think current laws inadequate for AI harms; two deepfake harassment/blackmail cases show barriers to justice. Calls AI harms a 'legal response gap'.
recommendations: Victim-centred legal reform, digital forensic capacity, AI liability rules, AI governance framework, digital literacy
quality_note: Perception survey (not victimisation); sampling not specified; low-tier journal

key_findings: Three forms: identity-based (body shaming, gender-nonconforming students labelled, regional accents), interactional aggression (sarcasm, exclusion of high achievers), technologically mediated manipulation (fake profiles sending fake nudes to family, deepfakes, doxing, strategic tagging). Memes/GIFs/emojis disguise hostility as humour. Most victims never report (fear of retaliation, privacy, futility).
author_gaps: Quantitative measurement of instances and impacts needed
recommendations: Anonymous campus reporting, anti-retaliation policy, peer support, teacher training, disciplinary action
quality_note: Good qualitative victim data; linguistics not criminology; purposive sample

key_findings: CSA 2026 lacks clear definitions and an ethical basis for AI-driven defamation/deepfakes; proposes codifying digital defamation via Islamic principles (Hifz al-Ird), discretionary (ta'zir) restorative punishment, and protecting sincere political criticism (nasiha).
recommendations: Shariah-informed definitions of digital defamation; restorative justice for deepfake victims; protect constructive criticism
quality_note: Written in Bangla (legacy SutonnyMJ font, text garbled in extraction); Islamic Studies authors; normative

key_findings: Lists attacks on Bangladeshi critical infrastructure (Sonali Bank 2013, Bangladesh Bank 2016, BPDB 2015, WannaCry at BERC 2017, DESCO prepaid-meter hack of 18,000 meters, Biman ransomware, Standard Chartered card fraud 2025); incidents under-reported and opaque. Compares US/UK/EU public-private partnership models.
recommendations: National Cyber Security Commission; PPP information sharing; transparent incident reporting; awareness campaigns
quality_note: Borderline (infrastructure security more than crime); relies heavily on one newspaper source (Wahid 2025); literature-only

key_findings: Mainly physical, psychological and financial COVID-era safety; DSA appears only briefly (one interviewee quote; cites Article 19: 60 DSA cases against 100 people incl. 22 journalists in Jan-May 2020).
prevalence_reported: Secondary: Article 19 2020 - 60 DSA cases, 100 people, 22 journalists
quality_note: Excluded at full text: DSA is a minor theme. Article 19 figure useful as background

key_findings: Digital evidence in general (Evidence (Amendment) Act 2022 s65B) assessed against Islamic evidentiary principles; proposes Shariah-Compliant Digital Evidence Framework. Not tied to cybercrime cases.
author_gaps: Empirical study of digital evidence use in courts; deepfake identification
quality_note: Excluded at full text: digital evidence in general, not cybercrime (per rule)

key_findings: All defamation is criminal in Bangladesh with no public/private figure distinction; DSA online defamation provisions allowed warrantless arrest and device seizure and were used against journalists, academics and opponents (many cases 2020-21), chilling debate.
recommendations: Decriminalise defamation; serious-harm threshold; public-figure 'actual malice' doctrine

location: Bogura; Rangpur; Natore; Sirajganj; Jamalpur; Rajshahi
key_findings: Delivery fraud against sellers (fake cash-on-delivery orders, refusals, fake returns) was the most consistent harm reported by all rural women F-commerce sellers; losses borne entirely by seller, no recourse against buyer or courier; coping = advance payment, blocking. Online harassment mainly from male customers adds emotional stress and triggers household suspicion; bKash/Nagad accounts often controlled by male relatives.
author_gaps: Urban-rural comparison; quantitative impact studies; platform algorithm effects
recommendations: Grievance redress for delivery fraud with couriers/platforms; Meta scam-profile warnings and reporting; collateral-free credit; digital rights training
quality_note: Seller-side fraud victimisation is rarely studied - useful gap evidence

key_findings: Comparative policy analysis on 5 dimensions; Bangladesh's NCSS 2023 judged more operationally detailed than Pakistan's 2021 NCSP (cybercrime units, reporting portal, MLATs); Pakistan's PECA criticised as speech-focused; both lack victim protection for individuals and e-commerce users.
recommendations: Funded research agenda, PPP mechanisms, curriculum integration, victim protection (directed at Pakistan)
quality_note: Pakistani author; treats Bangladesh mainly as benchmark; some claims about Bangladesh (e.g. MLAT partnerships) contradict R0039 - descriptive, uncritical of DSA

key_findings: Nationally representative: 6.6% of adolescents reported cyberbullying (verbal 31.6%, physical 20.8%); cyberbullying independently associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=1.15, p=0.012); cumulative bullying exposure shows graded association. No significant gender interaction for cyberbullying.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying victimisation 6.60% among 15-19 year olds (BAHWS 2019-20, n=9,116) - contrasts with ~32% in small convenience samples
recommendations: Comprehensive bullying prevention including online; accessible psychosocial services
quality_note: KEY PAPER: only nationally representative cyber-victimisation estimate so far; PLOS Mental Health; secondary analysis of public dataset (BAHWS) - usable for PhD

theory: none (crime prevention framing; notes lack of theory in Bangladesh prevention)
key_findings: Bangladesh scams dominated by institutional financial scams (e-commerce firms like Evaly, politically connected actors) with reactive, slow enforcement and no dedicated law; Singapore uses community interventions (ScamShield, anti-scam centre) against purchase, romance and impersonation scams.
author_gaps: Need for theoretical frameworks for scam prevention in Bangladesh
recommendations: Adopt Singapore-style anti-scam centre, public-private alerts, community awareness; dedicated anti-fraud law
quality_note: Dhaka University Studies with NUS/SIT co-authors; literature-only; conflates corporate e-commerce fraud with online scams

key_findings: Narrative synthesis of student cyber-awareness studies (India, Turkey, Indonesia etc.): awareness high, training and protective behaviour low.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: Pakistani authors, general international review; no Bangladesh analysis

key_findings: Descriptive account of cybercrime's economic cost and a speculative section on threats to environmental data; claims CIRT incidents rose from 10,500 (2019) to 24,600 (2023) and annual losses of BDT 500-600 crore.
prevalence_reported: Claimed CIRT incident counts 2019-2023 and BDT 500-600 crore annual loss - unverifiable
recommendations: Cyber security budget, SME support, DSA reform, international cooperation
quality_note: LOW QUALITY: rounded statistics not traceable to CIRT publications; several references appear fabricated; off-topic journal (Int J Environmental Sciences). Do not cite figures.

law_discussed: none (regulators: Bangladesh Bank, BTRC, Digital Security Agency)
key_findings: Case study of 2025 Standard Chartered OTP/SIM-swap scam: fraud arose at interfaces between banks, MFS, telcos and regulators; each actor 'followed protocol', victims left with blame-shifting; even educated users deceived by impersonation of bank officials. Proposes Multi-Actor Accountability Framework.
author_gaps: Quantitative modelling of fraud propagation; why informed users are deceived; evaluation of cross-institutional coordination
recommendations: Unified fraud reporting protocol; national digital-finance fraud intelligence platform; joint cyber-finance task force; shared liability
quality_note: Secondary/news-based case study; low-tier journal; useful conceptual framing of MFS/bank fraud governance gap

key_findings: Claims 27% could recognise phishing, 42% encountered attempts, 14% compromised (mainly fake job/scholarship offers), mean loss BDT 4,800; victims felt shame, withdrew online, rarely reported (stigma, distrust of justice).
recommendations: Curriculum cyber education, campaigns, victim support centres, legal reform, police training
quality_note: LOW QUALITY: very thin methods/results, no tables; same authors as R0141; several Bangladesh references appear fabricated (e.g. 'Journal of Digital Trust'); treat figures with caution

law_discussed: ICT Act 2006; Consumer Protection Act 2009; Penal Code; Digital Commerce Operation Guidelines 2018
key_findings: E-commerce fraud (advance-payment Facebook page scams, non-delivery, fake goods; complaints against Evaly etc.) surged after COVID; fragmented laws (Contract, Sale of Goods, Consumer Protection, ICT Act) with no dedicated e-commerce law; DNCRP complaints doubled.
recommendations: Dedicated e-commerce/online shopping law; amend Consumer Protection Act to name e-commerce; cyber courts; licensing of Facebook sellers

key_findings: Professionals rate outdated laws as the biggest obstacle (mean 4.3/5); few extradition treaties, little evidence sharing, MLATs rarely effective, JITs hard to form; forensic labs, encryption and investigator training weak.
author_gaps: Victim voices and comparative analysis missing; qualitative depth needed
recommendations: Law reform aligned to international norms, cyber courts, forensic labs, investigator/judge training, victim legal aid
quality_note: Descriptive Likert means only; some implausible statistics (median 43, SD 5.0) suggest careless reporting; new journal (IJCJ vol 1)

law_discussed: CSA 2023; DSA 2018; draft Personal Data Protection Act 2023
key_findings: CSA 2023 and draft data protection law lack consent standards, breach notification, clear limits on speech provisions and investigative capacity; benchmarked against GDPR and Budapest Convention.
recommendations: Comprehensive data protection law, breach notification duty, narrow speech offences, investigation capacity, accede to Budapest Convention
quality_note: Desk-based; translated text with errors (e.g. 'solar safety'); some news sources

key_findings: 90.5% of 295 DU students reported at least one form of cyber-victimisation (CYVIC 19-item scale, Bangla); 'often/always': social media ignoring 13.9%, offensive comments 12.4%, impersonation 7.9%, private images shared 4.5%, sextortion/blackmail with intimate material 2.6%, nude images recorded and shared 2.2%. No significant gender difference overall.
prevalence_reported: Any cyber-victimisation 90.5% (n=295, convenience sample); intimate-image blackmail 2.6% often/always, 18.4% rarely
recommendations: University anti-bullying policies, confidential reporting, counselling and peer support
quality_note: Validated scale; open data on OSF; convenience sample, single university; uses 'excluded non-victims' design oddly

key_findings: Fintech adoption and bank cybersecurity readiness overview; fraud only as a generic risk. Claims a 315-person survey but reports no results tables.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: fintech/security readiness, not crime; claimed methods not reported; several references appear fabricated

key_findings: Press freedom coverage during 2013 Shahbag period; Islamist groups most-cited barrier; social media central to coverage. No analysis of cyber laws or cyber offences.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: press freedom generally; appears recycled from an older (c.2014) study

key_findings: Inconsistent protective behaviour: most don't use 2FA, rarely update browsers or check privacy settings, many neutral on sharing personal info/accepting strangers; password, browser and social media practices each correlate with overall awareness.
prevalence_reported: none (no victimisation measured); cites Cyber Tribunal ~4,500 cases 2013-2021, mostly acquittals (bdnews24)
author_gaps: Small single-university sample; qualitative methods needed
recommendations: Curriculum cyber hygiene, workshops, password guidance
quality_note: Tag: awareness. Purposive sample at BUP; awareness outcome circularly built from same items

law_discussed: Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012; ICT Act 2006; CSA 2023; Penal Code
key_findings: 'Cyber slavery': Bangladeshis recruited via Facebook/TikTok/Telegram fake job ads and trafficked to Southeast Asian scam compounds, forced to run online fraud under torture; no law explicitly covers it - trafficking and cybercrime laws do not connect.
recommendations: Amend anti-trafficking law for online recruitment/digital coercion; regulate online job recruitment; joint trafficking-cyber units; victim rehabilitation
quality_note: Short, news-based. NEW THEME: scam-compound trafficking (victim-offender overlap) - emerging gap with almost no empirical research

key_findings: Among medical students, 48.3% reported cyberbullying victimisation (any frequency) and 39.5% admitted cyberbullying others; verbal (82%) and physical (73%) bullying more common; hostel environment, weak administration and student politics key drivers.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying victimisation 48.3%, perpetration 39.5% (n=632 medical students, convenience)
recommendations: Hostel supervision, reporting channels, counselling, enforcement
quality_note: Included at full text because it reports cyberbullying prevalence (rule for mental-health/bullying papers); rare perpetration figure; weak reporting (inconsistent percentages)

key_findings: Synthesises TF-VAW evidence: ActionAid 2022 - 63.5% of women harassed online; 78.7% TF-VAW (2025 roundtable); Ordinance 2025 s25 first defines sextortion, revenge porn, CSAM with enhanced penalties for women/children; Police Cyber Support for Women received 43,834 complaints to Feb 2025 but most victims don't file cases; rural women face access gap plus blackmail.
prevalence_reported: Secondary: 63.51% women harassed online (ActionAid 2022); PCSW 43,834 complaints 2020-Feb 2025
author_gaps: Research on distinct urban/rural women's needs
recommendations: Train police on Ordinance; anonymous reporting (USSD, drop boxes); digital safety help desks; digital ethics for boys/men; cyber clubs
quality_note: Short bulletin article; useful compilation of grey-literature statistics (PCSW complaint count is valuable administrative figure)

key_findings: Interpretive policy/discourse analysis: Bangladesh's cybersecurity narrative equates resilience with regime stability and reputation management (post-2016 heist, data breaches); ICT Act and DSA internalise state-centric control norms over transparency and citizen trust; ISO 27001/NIST adopted symbolically.
recommendations: Reframe cybersecurity around institutional legitimacy, social trust and professional identity

key_findings: Vulnerability assessment/penetration testing of 20 public and private university web infrastructures: widespread vulnerabilities, private universities more vulnerable; budget neglect makes universities a 'hacker playground'.
recommendations: Security hardening, regular VAPT, budget for university IT security
quality_note: Technical only (Tier A any field); Scopus-indexed journal

key_findings: Cybersecurity risk management in Islamic banks vs international standards; fraud and attacks only as generic risks (interviews mentioned in abstract only).
quality_note: Excluded at full text: organisational security readiness, not crime (consistent with R0175)

key_findings: Internet use and adolescent wellbeing post-COVID; cyberbullying mentioned only twice (abstract, literature), no measurement.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cyberbullying not measured (rule for mental-health papers)

location: international (India focus; Bangladesh Bank heist one of 4 cases)
key_findings: General review of financial-sector cyber threats; Bangladesh Bank heist one short case among Capital One, Equifax, Upstox.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: Indian author, generic review; Bangladesh one brief case (rule)

key_findings: Perceptions of Islamic law for preventing youth 'social crimes' (drugs, delinquency); cybercrime is one Likert item (mean 2.89).
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cybercrime one item in a list

theory: shrinking civic space; Mill's harm principle; Habermas' public sphere
key_findings: Vague cyber laws in Nepal (ETA, Social Media Bill), India (IT Act, UAPA) and Bangladesh (DSA, Ordinance) weaponised against journalists/activists (e.g. Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody under DSA); shutdowns, surveillance, platform censorship and criminal defamation form regional digital authoritarianism; violates ICCPR Art 19.
recommendations: Narrow definitions, judicial oversight, decriminalise defamation, regional digital-rights cooperation
quality_note: Nepali digital-rights practitioners; Bangladesh one of three substantive cases

sample_size: ~20 Bangladeshi + ~20 Indian interviewees; surveys; TikTok video content analysis
key_findings: UIUC PhD dissertation: Bangladeshi and Indian users perceive targeted ads through cultural/religious norms and are highly concerned about fraudulent ads; separate chapters analyse scam content on TikTok and GenAI-amplified fraud.
author_gaps: Non-Western users understudied in platform safety research
recommendations: Culture-aware platform design and ad/scam governance
quality_note: Borderline: Bangladesh is one of two interview samples; scam chapters not Bangladesh-specific. High-quality US dissertation

key_findings: Cyber-secure e-governance for SDG delivery; Bangladesh one of three cases; focus on governance architecture, not crime.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: e-governance security, not cybercrime; Indian authors, edited IIP volume

sample_size: 18 (12 rural fraud victims, 5 agents, 1 fintech expert)
key_findings: Rural MFS fraud victims depend on agents/relatives (sharing PINs), fall for calls impersonating MFS staff offering lower fees, SIM-swap fraud; little fraud-prevention knowledge; redress slow so small losses go unreported; agents and community leaders seen as key.
author_gaps: Larger quantitative and longitudinal studies; gender/income comparisons
recommendations: User-centred MFS interfaces, in-app fraud literacy, 2FA and alerts, stricter KYC (accounts on relatives' IDs), fraud response units
quality_note: RARE: primary data from MFS fraud victims (n=12) - but small, low-tier venue (Userhub)

sample_size: 1,410 DSA cases (4,404 accused) + 10 accused case studies
key_findings: CGS database of 1,410 DSA cases: 4,404 accused, 1,519 arrested (23.5 cases/month); average 3.12 accused per case - extrapolated to govt's 7,001 cases gives ~21,867 accused and ~7,542 arrested; police refuse to share data even under RTI; 10 case studies of accused show prolonged pre-trial detention, bail denial, financial ruin, social stigma; Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody.
prevalence_reported: 1,410 documented DSA cases, 4,404 accused, 1,519 arrests (Oct 2018-Sep 2023); govt figure 7,001 cases to Jan 2023
author_gaps: Official data withheld; cyber-tribunal data only covers trial stage
recommendations: Repeal DSA, release detainees, withdraw cases, transparency on case data
quality_note: KEY SOURCE: Ali Riaz/CGS (NED-funded) - the only systematic case dataset on cyber-law enforcement; grey literature; accused-side perspective

key_findings: Teenagers' perceptions of cybercrime consequences (88% loss of trust in transactions, 81% economic loss) and of cybercriminals' lifestyle (82% 'spend money lavishly', 67% 'ride the best cars'); social network users seen as prime victims (93%).
quality_note: Police Staff College author; very weak design (accidental sample, yes/no perception items), predatory outlet (J Clinical & Laboratory Research)

key_findings: In Bangla: Islamic guidance against cyberbullying; compiles Cyber Crime Awareness Foundation figures (cyberbullying 50.27% of cybercrime victims in 2023; account hacking 28.31%; 3.25% of victims died by suicide, 21% hid incidents) and PCSW (17,280 women contacted in first year); CSA 2023 provisions listed.
recommendations: Religious-moral education, blocking harmful sites, stricter law enforcement
quality_note: Bangla, SutonnyMJ font; normative; useful compilation of CCAF annual-report figures (a recurring NGO data source worth obtaining)

key_findings: Of 60 news posts on cyberbullying against women on outlet Facebook pages, 60% framed unfavourably to victims; 25% entertainment-framed, 20% crime; celebrities (30%) and police (15%) main sources, victims only 5%.
prevalence_reported: Cites DMP 2020: 80% of cyberbullying victims are women aged 14-22; BLAST 2017: 73% of women faced online harassment
recommendations: Victim-centred media coverage and awareness role
quality_note: UGC-funded; small purposive sample; relevant to media-as-data limitations

theory: feminist theory; stress and coping theory
key_findings: All 90 purposively sampled female students reported online harassment; inappropriate comments 83%, stalking 51%, sexual harassment 42%, threats 36%, hacking/impersonation 24%; Facebook 88%, Messenger 74%; sleep disturbance 49% moderate+, suicidal thoughts 3.3%.
prevalence_reported: 100% victimisation (purposive n=90 - not a prevalence estimate)
recommendations: Cyberbullying policies in institutions, counselling, helplines, platform accountability, regular surveys
quality_note: Co-author is CID Additional DIG (police link). Purposive sample of victims inflates 'prevalence'; frequency table internally inconsistent

theory: routine activity theory; lifestyle-exposure theory; cyber-lifestyle routine activities (Reyns)
key_findings: Typology of women's victimisation on social networking sites in Bangladesh (cyberbullying, morphing, Facebook cloning, account hacking, intimate-image blackmail, hidden cameras, romance fraud, 'virtual rape'); causes: oversharing, weak privacy settings, inadequate laws, platform non-response; explained through RAT/lifestyle theory (suitable targets, absent guardianship).
prevalence_reported: Secondary: BNWLA 2014 - 65 suicide attempts by female victims 2010-14; >17,000 telecom complaints by Dec 2017, 70% from women
author_gaps: Few Bangladesh studies on causes and patterns of women's SNS victimisation
recommendations: Privacy awareness, report to cyber police, platform action
quality_note: FIRST paper to apply criminological theory (RAT/lifestyle) - but only conceptually, no data; victim-blaming language ('soft-mentality'); author is victimology PhD researcher at DU

key_findings: Claimed PRISMA-based review plus survey/interviews on sector-wide impacts of cybercrime (banking, finance) in Bangladesh; motives classified as financial, political, espionage; legal frameworks judged inadequate.
recommendations: Strengthen law enforcement capacity and cybersecurity measures
quality_note: IMPORTANT for our review: an earlier 'PRISMA' review of Bangladesh cybercrime exists - must be cited and differentiated (ours is a scoping review with transparent search and charting). Methods vague; predatory-leaning publisher (Learning Gate)

law_discussed: Bangladesh Bank MFS Regulations 2022; Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012
key_findings: Bangladesh Bank MFS regulations rely on weak KYC (anyone with another person's NID details can access/open accounts) and a reactive risk-based model, enabling MFS fraud and illicit financial flows (IFF).
recommendations: Smart regulation; stronger e-KYC/biometric verification; proactive supervision
quality_note: Univ. of Pecs yearbook (Hungary); cited by R0239. Links MFS fraud to KYC/NID misuse - same mechanism police describe in R0241

key_findings: Case studies of Shahidul Alam (detained), cartoonist Ahmed Kabir Kishore (custodial torture), Mushtaq Ahmed (custodial death) and filmmaker Saddam Hossen show ICT s57 -> DSA -> CSA used to silence academics, journalists and artists, producing a culture of fear.
quality_note: Indiana University PhD student; SCIRP journal; case-based

key_findings: Overview of white-collar crime (embezzlement, corruption, money laundering); cybercrime/digital fraud one item among several.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cybercrime one item in a list; low-tier journal

theory: none (regime type / spiral of silence framing)
key_findings: Survey of Facebook users incl. journalists, opposition activists, academics: restrictive regime structure and DSA increase self-censorship; higher education associated with more self-censorship; 'climate of fear' x critical content interaction intensifies it; gender minimal effect.
quality_note: Univ. of Bergen author; small purposive sample; quantitative evidence on chilling effect (rare)

key_findings: NLP sentiment model for AML/CFT adverse-media screening in an MFS (94.6% weighted accuracy); about money laundering compliance, not cybercrime.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: AML compliance tool, not cybercrime

population: general public; police or justice actors
sample_size: 50 (public, people involved in scams, police - breakdown not reported)
location: nr (mentions Madhupur-Tangail, Gazipur, Dhaka scam hubs)
key_findings: Romance scams rising; claims interviews with victims, people involved in scams and police; scammers clustered in Madhupur (Tangail), Gazipur, Dhaka; victims ashamed to report; laws lack a romance-fraud offence; police lack training and tools for transnational cases.
recommendations: Define online dating fraud in law, train police, public awareness
quality_note: Only paper so far claiming OFFENDER interviews - but methods written in future tense, results only report demographics (n=50, low-income, low-education); thematic findings not shown. New journal (vol 1)

key_findings: Trolling used to embarrass, intimidate and silence TV actors, theatre performers and rural artists in Bangladesh; causes psychological distress, depression and alienation; framed as human rights violation.
recommendations: Empower artists, platform moderation, supportive digital environment
quality_note: Small sample; international author team (India, Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia); new victim group (artists)

key_findings: Anthropology of mobile phone regulation, SIM registration and cybercrime legislation in Papua New Guinea.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: PNG study; Bangladesh only cited (Huang 2017)

key_findings: 'Sextortion' here means corruption-linked sexual coercion when accessing water/sanitation services (offline), not online image-based extortion.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: keyword false positive (offline sextortion); good-quality UNU-MERIT study

key_findings: Regression: social influence, social media use, internet addiction, social anxiety and trait anger all positively predict cyberbullying (outcome ambiguous between perpetration and involvement).
recommendations: Awareness, online safety guidance for students
quality_note: MBA student author; one of few studies on predictors of cyberbullying behaviour (offending-side), but construct unclear

key_findings: Tests DSA restrictions against constitutional 'reasonable restrictions' (Art 39): cyber defamation and sedition provisions are the law's real (in-situ) focus, cyberspace safety secondary; restrictions fail reasonableness and are unconstitutional.
quality_note: Author from private industry; SCIRP Beijing Law Review; long doctrinal piece

law_discussed: Digital Commerce Operation Guidelines 2021; DSA 2018; Consumer Rights Protection Act 2009
theory: regulation theory (risk-based vs strategic enforcement, Bluff)
key_findings: E-commerce Ponzi-like frauds (Evaly, Alesha Mart, Orange, Dhamaka, Qcoom; ~$152m allegedly siphoned) exploited predatory pricing and delayed delivery; Digital Commerce Guidelines 2021 non-binding, CRPA doesn't cover online transactions, DSA has no e-commerce/IFF provisions, no cross-border rules.
prevalence_reported: Secondary: ~$152m allegedly siphoned by e-commerce firms
recommendations: Strategic enforcement model; rules on predatory pricing, complaints and cross-border e-commerce
quality_note: Companion to R0263 (same author, Pecs yearbook); corporate e-commerce fraud - distinct type from individual online scams

key_findings: Policy brief synthesising BSMMU team's studies: ~1 in 2 child internet users sexually abused online; vulgar friend requests 47%, sexual propositions 35%, porn texts 29%, requests for nude images 18%; rural 21% received explicit messages; urban children twice the odds; each extra hour online OR 1.09; no specific online CSA offence in law; Child Affairs desks not implemented; media exposes child victims.
prevalence_reported: Secondary (Salwa et al.; Mubassara et al.): ~50% online sexual abuse among child internet users; 21% rural children received sexually explicit messages
recommendations: Criminalise online CSA/grooming explicitly; train police; school curriculum; ISP filters; age verification; join Interpol ICSE/VICC
quality_note: BSMMU public health group (Atiqul Haque) has a programme of online child abuse studies (R0202, R0281 likely same team) - potential collaborators

key_findings: Nationwide survey of school-going adolescents during COVID: 15.9% reported being cyberbullied by classmates (single item); cyberbullied students had 63% vs 32% moderate+ depression; cyberbullying AOR 2.67 for anxiety.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying by classmates 15.88% (n=3,571; single yes/sometimes item)
recommendations: School mental health and anti-cyberbullying programmes
quality_note: Included at full text: reports prevalence (rule). icddr,b-led, PLOS ONE; large nationwide (not strictly probability) sample - second-best prevalence source after R0107

key_findings: Conference abstract on internet addiction; cyberbullying mentioned once.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: abstract only, not cybercrime

data_source: technical dataset (OWASP ZAP scans of 30 websites)
key_findings: 51 alerts on 30 sites: 6 high risk (SQLi, PII disclosure, path traversal, hash disclosure, cloud metadata), 14 medium, 18 low. Earlier work cited: 64% of BD sites have common vulnerabilities and 309 of 359 education sites are SQLi-vulnerable. Context given: 50M-citizen NID leak (2023) and hacktivist defacements from India and Myanmar.
author_gaps: Few sites covered; some sites returned zero alerts (possibly a scanner limit); academic and e-commerce sites not covered
recommendations: Mitigations for the top 8 vulnerabilities; government attention to web security
quality_note: Single automated scanner with no manual verification; vulnerable sites anonymised; mid-tier MECS outlet. Useful as attack-surface context only.

data_source: social media data (3.2M Facebook comments, 8 pages; ToxLex_bn on Mendeley)
key_findings: Toxic bigrams fall into 8 classes. Misogynist (19% of types) and sexist/patriarchal (30%) bullying dominate. Political hate is 14% of tokens; religious/communal hate is 4% of tokens but over 7% of types. Women celebrities' pages get mostly misogynist abuse, while news pages carry political and communal hate (India-Bangladesh, Hindu-Muslim, 1971). Users alter spellings to evade filters.
prevalence_reported: content prevalence (toxic token share), not victimisation
author_gaps: Romanised Bangla (Banglish) not covered; single annotator, so no inter-rater agreement; no source sentences
recommendations: Use the lexicon for platform filters and ML models; template for other Indic languages
quality_note: Single author, preprint, single annotator. A large real-world corpus is a strength. Evidence of gendered online abuse at scale.

key_findings: Describes online religious rumours that set off mob violence (Ramu 2012, Nasirnagar 2016, Comilla/Pirganj 2021). The Nasirnagar victim was himself charged under the ICT Act. BTRC blocked about 300 IDs in days after Comilla. Cites Al-Zaman: religious rumours rose from 5% (2017) to 40% (2020) of rumours. Sets out DSA s.28 penalties.
recommendations: Verify before sharing; more BTRC and police monitoring and fast takedown; awareness via religious leaders; an interfaith verification response team
quality_note: Low quality: new US predatory-style outlet, no method beyond desk review, a generic list of crime types copied from Indian sources. Useful only for the case chronology of online religious rumour violence.

key_findings: SEM survey on the behavioural drivers of bank scams (greed, rationalisation, loan-default culture). The scams are insider/loan fraud; online banking fraud appears only in the literature review.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: offline white-collar bank fraud, not cybercrime

key_findings: 80% of journalists had never heard of deepfakes; only 9% got any input from their employer (a short talk, no training); none knew a detection method or a training institute. 81% see Facebook as the main spreader; 95% want media-house initiatives and 100% want a regulator. Cites the DSA: about 900 cases in 26 months, 40% against journalists.
prevalence_reported: awareness: 20% had heard of deepfakes, n=100
recommendations: Deepfake training by media houses; a technology-journalism course in journalism schools; government training
quality_note: IISTE (predatory-listed) outlet; descriptive percentages only; sampling only loosely described as random. Early BD deepfake data point (2022).

key_findings: 78% of students say the DSA works against free expression and 90% want it amended, yet 91% support legal punishment for online hate and harassment and 57% say the DSA builds responsibility. 30.6% had been threatened for posting views. Experts criticise vague terms, police powers, multiple cases in different districts and use against Baul singers.
prevalence_reported: 30.6% threatened for sharing views online, n=200
recommendations: Amend the DSA (one expert says repeal); digital media literacy in textbooks; train cyber police; a tolerant political culture
quality_note: Convenience student sample; descriptive only; low-tier journal. Shows the ambivalence: people want protection from online harm but fear the speech law.

key_findings: Bangladesh case: journalist Supriti Dhar (Women Chapter) faced online threats and offline stalking after the Shahbagh protests and blogger murders. Police told her to write on 'safe topics'; she went into exile in Sweden and still faces a DSA case. The paper argues online threats and offline violence form a continuum and silence women.
recommendations: Platforms should regulate abuse more effectively
quality_note: Journalistic essay in a feminist journal; Bangladesh is one case of five. Shows the victim being criminalised under the DSA and a police non-response.

key_findings: Of 59 cybersecurity items in two top dailies, 63% were event-driven, 5 investigative and 9 awareness-raising. Only 24% were written by staff; most were translated foreign stories, and Kaler Kantho cited 'Internet' as the source for 18 items. There was little coverage of Bangladesh's own incidents.
recommendations: More investigative and awareness journalism on cybersecurity
quality_note: Small 3-month sample of two papers; inconsistent study year (2019 vs 2020). Relevant to using news as a data source: BD press coverage of cybercrime is thin and largely imported.

data_source: news reports; secondary literature; official statistics
key_findings: Policy paper on e-commerce cyber risk. BD e-commerce grew from Tk 4bn (2016) to Tk 70bn (2021). Case stories of deep-discount and Ponzi frauds (Evaly, e-orange): money stuck in escrow and a weak government response, which it reads as unpreparedness. Users are largely unaware of risks. Global breach examples are padded in.
recommendations: Social campaigns; a school curriculum chapter; train law enforcers; stronger e-commerce security; a law defining cybercrimes; institutional cyber governance
quality_note: Low-tier Indonesian law journal; 'case study' consists of news stories; much padding with Indian/global examples. Overlaps with R0332 on e-commerce Ponzi fraud.

data_source: technical dataset (Acunetix + ZAP scans of 25 websites)
key_findings: Acunetix found 133 high, 466 medium and 500 low alerts across 25 anonymised government/financial sites; ZAP found far fewer. Top flaws: clickjacking (20 sites), misconfiguration (19), CSRF (15), information disclosure (14), XSS (11); SQLi on 4. Cites the Bangladesh Bank heist ($101m lost) and Kaspersky 2020 ranking BD 8th for online infection.
author_gaps: Few sites; extend to education and e-commerce
recommendations: PHP mitigations for the top 5 vulnerabilities
quality_note: Undergraduate team, MECS outlet; the same design is repeated in R0348 (cited as its ref 11). Attack-surface context only.

key_findings: F-commerce adoption under COVID (SEM-PLS). Fraudulent sellers who fail to deliver are mentioned only in passing as a trust issue.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: adoption/trust study (rule: fintech or e-commerce adoption excluded)

key_findings: Dhaka University students in COVID: most victimisation came from strangers on Facebook and other social media (39.4%), then fellow students (18.9%). Victims reported harm to assignments, grades, missed classes, family problems, anxiety and depression, and suicidal thoughts (29.4% of female and 17.2% of male victims). Women reported a wider range of harms; few reported to university officials.
prevalence_reported: not clearly reported (says 'a major number' of women victimised at least once), n=100
author_gaps: Research on cyberbullying among undergraduates is underdeveloped
quality_note: Purposive Facebook sample of 100; tables are confusing (column percentages sum to 100 within each category); no inferential statistics; references duplicated. Weak but adds a gender and stranger-perpetrator signal.

key_findings: Ranks 11 IT-system failure factors in BD banks; cyber-attack and database hacking rank highest, alongside server failure and network outages.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: organisational IT-risk prioritisation, not cybercrime (rule: organisational readiness papers excluded)

key_findings: Global PRISMA review of cybersecurity and compliance models in finance; Bangladesh appears only as the SWIFT heist case example.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: not Bangladesh-focused, and organisational. Dubious new outlet; the PDF header names a different paper.

key_findings: 82% claim to understand cybercrime but only 37% recognise terms like malware or key-logger. 18% personally know an e-commerce fraud victim; 32% distrust e-commerce platforms; 78% want stronger laws; 88% want awareness campaigns. Uses the fraud triangle to argue that youth unemployment (pressure), weak security (opportunity) and rationalisation drive offending, but tests none of this.
prevalence_reported: 18% know an e-commerce fraud victim, n=120
author_gaps: Small sample; little prior Bangladesh research on the determinants of cybercrime
recommendations: Awareness campaigns; stronger laws; e-commerce security steps (HTTPS, passwords); youth employment
quality_note: Low-quality outlet; 'systematic review' and 'grounded theory' are claimed but not done; descriptive yes/no items. One of the few to name an offending theory (fraud triangle), applied only conceptually.

key_findings: Bank directors rate IT governance and IT investment as the top cyber risks; most boards have no IT committee or IT-expert director, and many banks have no CIO.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: organisational cyber-risk governance (rule: organisational readiness excluded). A possible context citation on bank governance weaknesses.

key_findings: Women Facebook sellers get porn links, threats and obscene comments while advertising; blocking is the only response they use. Also: hoax orders and couriered goods refused (seller-side fraud), illicit groups (weed, sex toys) operating with no regulation, and family and connectivity barriers. Cites a Dhaka Tribune claim that 70% of women facing cyber harassment are aged 15-25.
recommendations: Government should be 'rigid' on cyberbullying; training by government and NGOs; regulate and tax F-commerce
quality_note: Undergraduate authors, low-tier outlet, thin analysis. Corroborates R0096 on seller-side victimisation and adds the gendered harassment of women entrepreneurs.

key_findings: Women-safety Android app (SOS, siren, law bot) for mainly offline violence; cyberbullying appears only in a list of harms.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: offline VAW safety app; online harm is one item in a list

key_findings: Experts see DSA ss.8, 21, 25, 28, 29, 31, 32 (esp. s.32 on 'computer spying') as chilling investigative journalism; the Editors' Council objected. Cites 1,417 ICT Act cases 2006-June 2017, 65% under s.57, and argues the DSA inherited s.57's substance. Presents the government view (protects users) alongside.
recommendations: Amend the problematic sections; protective practices for investigative journalists
quality_note: Only 5 KIIs; largely a review of commentary; Turkish low-tier outlet. A useful figure: 1,417 ICT Act cases, 65% under s.57.

key_findings: Generic overview of cybercrime types and ICT Act ss.57, 66-68. Bangladesh-specific claims: the RAB website hack, secret filming in cyber-cafe cabins posted online, BTRC 'overwhelmed with thousands of complaints', and the Cyber Tribunal set up after the Ramu violence. Argues the ICT Act is poorly implemented for lack of awareness and capacity.
recommendations: A specific cyber law; cyber police stations and training (Mumbai cyber lab model); NGO and private funding; awareness and user precautions
quality_note: Very low quality: large passages lifted from blogs and Malaysian assignment sites (refs are blogspot/slideshare; a 'Hacker Hotshot' side note left in the text). Outdated (internet users given as 3 million). Cite only with caution.

key_findings: Argues for forensic accounting against white-collar financial crime (Destiny 2000, Hallmark-Sonali, People's Leasing); the BB heist is mentioned only in passing.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: offline financial/accounting fraud

key_findings: Grade 8-10 students: 43% cyberbullied outside school and 43% inside; about 43% admit perpetrating, males more. Only 5% would tell a teacher and none got help from school staff; 71% knew no cyber-safety strategy; 90% want it in the curriculum. Reasons for not telling: fear of getting into trouble, staff won't act, or parents will restrict internet use.
author_gaps: Little Bangladesh research on school cyberbullying; rural students unfamiliar with the terms
recommendations: School ICT policies; cyberbullying in the curriculum; Bengali-language materials; parent involvement
quality_note: Tiny sample (n=21) used to report percentages; exploratory only. Notable for asking about both victimisation and perpetration, and about reporting behaviour.

key_findings: General essay on violence against women; cybercrime (cyberstalking, filmed rape spread online) is one cause in a list of seven.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: online harm is one item in a list

sample_size: nr (small Google Form survey, ~19 implied by percentages)
key_findings: 36.8% of female Facebook users surveyed report harassment, mostly from new online contacts. Case vignettes (from the Daily Star) cover sextortion of a 16-year-old leading to a suicide attempt, a morphed nude photo, and Facebook refusing to remove a page. Women don't report out of shame; police are bribed or pressured. Cites the minister's claim that 73% of women internet users face cybercrime. Claims Facebook is used for trafficking recruitment (fake romance) without Bangladeshi evidence.
recommendations: Privacy settings; enforce cyber laws without bias; victims should report; social support rather than humiliation
quality_note: Undergraduate paper; n not reported; vignettes from news. Early (2017) source on non-reporting and the minister's 73% claim.

key_findings: Describes the ransomware trend and claims BD sites are vulnerable (no data shown despite the abstract); recounts the BB heist; 'no ransom demand heard yet' in BD (2017).
recommendations: Teacher and student training, backups, refuse to pay ransom, government data backups
quality_note: Very weak: student paper, references largely irrelevant (e-health, batteries), no vulnerability data despite claims. Context only.

key_findings: Chronology of nationalist hacktivist defacement 'wars'. BD vs India: Bangladesh Cyber Army and Black Hat Hackers defaced 1,100+ Indian sites after the BSF killing of Felani Khatun (Jan 2012), with about 3,000 more in 2013 and Indian retaliation. BD vs Pakistan from Dec 2012 (Cyber71, Grey Hat Hackers). Triggers are border killings, cricket and anniversaries. Also covers the BB heist.
recommendations: Strong IT policy; regional cyber-security law
quality_note: Descriptive chronology from tech blogs and hacker claims; IR framing. A rare source on Bangladeshi offenders (hacktivist groups and their motives) relevant to an offender-side gap.

key_findings: Cost model for implementing information security standards (Lithuania); the BB heist is mentioned once in the abstract.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: not about Bangladesh

key_findings: 90% of purposively sampled girls report victimisation (10% no answer); Facebook is the main channel (58%). Causes given: relationship break-ups (26%) and 'moral degradation'. 80% say victimisation leads to early marriage and school dropout; 60% say victims hide it from family out of fear; 50% don't know the law. Case of 'Rabeya' who attempted suicide. Victim-blaming framing ('self-display of girls').
recommendations: Effective legal framework; culture of law compliance; family and social support
quality_note: Student paper; purposive sample; percentage tables inconsistent; moralising, victim-blaming causes. The early-marriage link (80%) is an unusual claim worth noting but weakly evidenced. Cited by R0486.

law_discussed: Anti-Terrorism Act 2009;draft Cyber Security Act 2015;Constitution Art 43
key_findings: Militants (Ansarullah Bangla Team) use Facebook and the internet for propaganda and recruitment; the 2012 Ramu attack was planned on Facebook; blogger killings. The state is buying mass surveillance tools. Art 43 privacy is weak and there is no privacy law; draft CSA 2015 s.14 penalises privacy breach by private individuals only, not state organs, with no compensation.
recommendations: Explicit surveillance law on legality and proportionality; independent prior authorisation and oversight; compensation for state privacy breaches; online counter-narratives
quality_note: BUP law lecturers, IOSR (predatory-listed) outlet. Early analysis of the 2015 cyber-security draft, the forerunner of the DSA. Relevant to state surveillance as an under-studied side.

key_findings: Manual SQLi testing of .bd sites: 400 of 600 vulnerable to basic SQLi; 309 of 359 education sites vulnerable (63% fully compromisable); of 108 financial sites, 80% of bank sites had no protection against basic SQLi; 379 of 526 vulnerable to base64/variable SQLi. ITU GCI 2014 gave Bangladesh 0.29 (2nd in South Asia). bdCERT exists but there are no national certification frameworks.
recommendations: Developer training; national cyber-security framework; public awareness; monitoring
quality_note: DIU/NSU team; source of the figures cited by R0348 and R0374. Ethical issue: active exploitation of live sites without stated authorisation. Context only.

key_findings: E-commerce security and privacy satisfaction among SMEs; findings concern adoption barriers (infrastructure, slow internet); the cybercrime paragraph repeats generic news items.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: e-commerce adoption and satisfaction (rule)

key_findings: Early (2012) victimisation survey of young cybercafe users: 23% gave personal data to 'tempting offers', 95% of PC owners had virus infections, 1 in 30 had been hacked, and none reported financial loss or threats. Cases: an advance-fee (419) email scam asking for $3,000 and a fake US green-card offer. Women were largely absent from cybercafes for safety reasons. Also notes there is no chronological Bangladeshi cybercrime data.
prevalence_reported: 3.3% hacked; 23% disclosed data to scam offers, n=30
author_gaps: No chronological cybercrime data in Bangladesh
quality_note: SUST sociology; tiny accidental sample. Historically important as the earliest Bangladeshi cyber-victimisation survey (widely cited, e.g. by R0486 and R0527); a baseline for change over time.

key_findings: Indian mobile banking fraud law (RBI circulars, case law); Bangladesh appears only through the SWIFT heist case study.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: India-focused (could be considered for Tier B, but is out of scope there as a predatory-listed legal essay; the abstract is already captured)

key_findings: Women see deepfakes as weapons, not fun. A Rajshahi student was forced out of student organisations and told by her mother to quit studies after a face-swapped sexual image circulated; another woman's ex sent intimate videos to her new husband. Women are presumed guilty even when content is known to be fake. Low verification ability; police blame victims ('why did you share photos?'), so silence is chosen over reporting.
author_gaps: Small, internet-connected sample; no rural women; no platform, police or policy perspectives
recommendations: Contestation mechanisms (labels, rapid takedown); trauma-aware reporting; culturally grounded literacy; privacy-by-design
quality_note: Strong team (Sultana, Ahmed, Haque); arXiv 2026 work-in-progress. Best qualitative evidence so far on deepfake image abuse and police secondary victimisation.

key_findings: The Evidence Act 1872 (amended 2022) has no provisions for AI-generated content, synthetic-media authentication or deepfake expert qualification. Neither the UK nor Malaysia has a deepfake-specific regime, but Malaysia offers certification and the UK a reliability inquiry. Notes the CSA 2026's move to regulate AI-generated content.
recommendations: Sequential authentication framework; a national digital-evidence and deepfake forensics unit (e.g. under the BCC); accreditation for forensic experts; calibrated rather than reflexive suspicion
quality_note: Low-tier outlet (IRE) but current (Sept 2026) and directly on the CSA 2026. Useful for the courts/evidence gap.

key_findings: Doctrinal review: laws on MFS and e-commerce fraud are fragmented and reactive, and are not designed for platform commerce or fintech. Fraud types: phishing and vishing impersonating banks or MFS, payment scams, identity theft, unauthorised transactions, non-delivery.
recommendations: Coherent digital-fraud law; institutional coordination; consumer redress
quality_note: Short doctrinal piece, low-tier outlet (2026). Corroborates the regulatory-fragmentation theme; no empirical data.

key_findings: Narrative secondary-data review: harassment, impersonation, outing and non-consensual intimate content disproportionately affect women. Persistence is driven by low digital literacy, weak enforcement and gender norms. Underreporting is noted; statistics are not comparable across sources, so no prevalence is estimated.
author_gaps: Inconsistent definitions and samples across sources
recommendations: Implement existing law; digital literacy; reporting and support systems; challenge gender norms
quality_note: New low-tier outlet (2026); non-systematic review. Names the online disinhibition effect only conceptually.

key_findings: Cross-cutting themes: deepfakes target women and marginalised groups; platform moderation fails for South Asian languages (Bengali); institutional recourse is inaccessible; participants prefer locally governed solutions. Bangladesh has no deepfake-specific law, and the DSA is criticised as actively harmful rather than protective.
recommendations: Survivor support; linguistic justice in moderation; community-governed Trust and Safety
quality_note: Journal of Online Trust and Safety; reputable HCI team (Gamage); Bangladesh is one of 3 cases (n=12). Complements R0007.

key_findings: Global desk review of election deepfakes; the Bangladesh January 2024 election is mentioned in one table row.
quality_note: Excluded at full text: Bangladesh incidental; low-tier outlet

data_source: police or court records (94 official complaints)
theory: crime script analysis (Cornish); routine activity theory; situational crime prevention; crime pattern theory
key_findings: Hybrid 'pig-butchering' investment scams. Total loss BDT 91m; median BDT 648k; Gini 0.51; the top 10% of cases account for 34% of losses (90% bank+MFS, 9/10 male, mean age 41). Median loss for MFS-only cases is BDT 153k versus BDT 838k for bank+MFS. Five-stage script: fake personas, then approach via Facebook/WhatsApp/Telegram, then small MFS deposits, then larger bank transfers, then cash-out. The switch from mobile wallet to bank is a key 'pinch point'. Links to scam-compound trafficking of Bangladeshis (Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos) come from external sources only.
author_gaps: Underreporting; no data on offender networks; crypto cases too few; self-report errors
recommendations: Controls at the MFS-to-bank transition; prioritise high-loss cases and hotspots; early cross-border cooperation; integrated environmental-criminology prevention
quality_note: KEY PAPER: authored by Bangladesh Police and Bangladesh Bank officers (Research Square preprint, Dec 2025). First police-data crime-script study of Bangladeshi cyber fraud, and the first real criminological theory application with data. Shows that police complaint data can be accessed via insiders. Directly relevant to an MFS-fraud PhD.

key_findings: LGBTQIA+ people in Bangladesh and India face online blackmail, threats and outing; weak legal protection plus criminalisation (s.377) and stigma deepen harm and silence victims.
recommendations: National anti-bullying policies; school networks; recognise online harassment as a human-rights violation
quality_note: Student author, predatory-listed outlet (IJRAR). The only paper so far on LGBTQIA+ online victimisation in Bangladesh, marking a clear population gap.

key_findings: Describes juvenile 'gangs' using TikTok/Likee for trafficking ('TikTok Hridoy' case in Bangalore), Facebook drug-selling groups, and students running an online porn ring. Police HQ claim of 500+ juvenile gangs. Cyber Tribunal caseload rose from 3 (2013) to 721 (2019); 2,642 cases sent from police since 2013; of 1,082 cases filed directly, 635 were dismissed; 4,657 DSA cases in 3 years. Tribunals expanded from 1 to 8 in 2021.
recommendations: Curriculum; NID verification for apps and SIMs; try juvenile cyber-offenders as adults; district-level tribunals
quality_note: Co-authored by a Senior Judicial Magistrate; same new US outlet as R0356; news-sourced. Recommendations are punitive and questionable (prosecuting juveniles as adults). Useful offender-side and tribunal caseload figures.

data_source: legal texts; official statistics; secondary literature
key_findings: Socio-legal review: legislative progress is substantial but institutional capacity to investigate, prosecute and adjudicate cyber offences lags.

PRISMA 2020 systematic review (8 databases, 2020–2026) of MFS fraud in six South Asian countries: social engineering, OTP interception, SIM swap, account takeover, agent collusion; detection methods and policy responses.
quality_note: Competing/adjacent review to ours (MFS-specific) – must be cited and differentiated. Abstract only.

key_findings: Traces ICT Act → DSA → CSA 2023 → Cyber Security Ordinance 2025 and their human-rights effects; laws justified by real cyber threats but used against expression.

theory: secondary victimisation; procedural justice; access to justice
key_findings: Victim-survivors of image-based abuse and sextortion use silence and delayed disclosure as protective strategies; institutional responses produce secondary victimisation; understandings of justice evolve beyond formal prosecution.
quality_note: KEY: rare criminological, theory-informed empirical study with victims and stakeholders (2026). Directly supports gap G3 (reporting). Abstract only – seek full text.

key_findings: Protocol for a TFGBV scoping review in Bangladesh (masculinities lens). Cites the Violence Against Women Survey 2024: just over 8% of women with technology access report lifetime TFGBV.
quality_note: Protocol only, not a completed study. IMPORTANT: a parallel Bangladesh TFGBV scoping review is planned – cite and differentiate (ours is broader: all cybercrime, South Asia, bibliometric). VAW Survey 2024 is a key national prevalence source.

key_findings: Global cybercrime law textbook; Bangladesh Bank heist is one case study.
Facebook, WhatsApp, Telegram and TikTok used to organise financial fraud, drug trafficking, cyberbullying, blackmail and extremist content; mixed methods (content analysis, survey, cases).
quality_note: Preprint; sample sizes not in abstract.

key_findings: Qualitative secondary analysis of unlawful AI use (nature, classification, threats) in Bangladesh and worldwide.
Media control after the July 2024 uprising; CSA used to threaten journalists; climate of fear persists (journalist suicide note).
Cybersecurity awareness does not always translate into safe online behaviour among university students (Bangladesh vs Finland, Likert survey).
DSA used to suppress dissent and monitor activity, producing self-censorship among citizens, journalists and activists.
State–corporate nexus in cyber surveillance in Bangladesh and India; laws and securitised discourse justify surveillance that erodes privacy and civil liberties.
Forensic accounting in professional education; cybercrime listed only among fraud types.
Youth participation in financial markets and institutional transparency; adoption/trust.

Online violence against young digitally active women perceived as highly prevalent; many experience multiple forms (harassment, impersonation, hate speech, stalking, sextortion); low legal awareness; weak institutional response.
2016 Bangladesh Bank heist as an outcome of macro (governance, geopolitics), meso (ecosystem) and micro (organisational) weaknesses, not only technical intrusion.
Suicidal tendencies among students; abstract does not report cyberbullying prevalence.
Policy brief comparing Bangladesh speech-regulating cyber laws (2006–2026) with Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia on six criteria; asks whether security-justified laws function as executive control.
Women entrepreneurs navigate online and in-person harassment and crime, including via payment platforms; banking tools embed gender discrimination.
Body image disturbance among students; cyber harm not central.
Bangladeshi female gamers face sexist, marginalising messages and cyberbullying shaped by moral policing; describe emotional impacts and coping strategies.
Institutional fraud via manipulated insiders and AI; no Bangladesh focus.
TFGBV across five South Asian countries (incl. Bangladesh) as a spillover of patriarchal violence; doctrinal plus qualitative analysis of legal and socio-cultural responses.
Cybercrime as an emerging threat to commercial banks in Bangladesh; technical limitations and capacity gaps.
Deepfakes cause women mental distress, reputational harm, fear of online participation and distrust of law; informal support networks compensate for weak institutions.
Nationally representative BAHWS data: cyberbullying associated with major depressive disorder among female adolescents (multiple logistic regression).
quality_note: National secondary data; same source as R0107.

key_findings: Blockchain/smart-contract architecture proposed to reduce e-commerce fraud in Bangladesh.
Cross-sectional survey of social, psychological and academic effects of cyberbullying on university students.
Journal issue editorial introducing four articles (one on Bangladesh banking).
US dissertation on deepfake detection tools for journalists; no Bangladesh focus in abstract.
Phenomenological study of young adults' lived experiences of Facebook cyberbullying in Dhaka.
Narrative/awareness piece built around one teenager's story.
Integrative review of cyber threats to Bangladeshi banks (phishing, ransomware, hacking, insider attacks) linked to legacy systems, outdated regulation and skills shortages.
Overview of cyber-security governance obligations under the ICT Act 2006 and CSA 2023.
Deep-learning hate-speech detection on Bangladeshi social media.
Cyber Protection Ordinance 2025 lacks a functional definition of AI, liability attribution and enforceable ethical safeguards.
Mental health of women F-commerce entrepreneurs; abstract does not centre online harm.
Offline bank loan fraud and perpetrator motivation.
Gen Z social media attitudes and norms; cyber harm not central.
Online activism against (offline) violence against women.
Consumer protection gaps for e-commerce fraud, misleading ads and data privacy under the CRPA 2009, CSA 2023 and Digital Commerce Guidelines.
'Dual State' thesis: Digital Bangladesh rhetoric alongside AI-enabled surveillance and suppression of dissent (2014–2024).
Suicidal expression on social media; not cybercrime.
